cases.interviewerQuestion: What made you realize the undifferentiated store was the actual root cause, rather than just patching each stale-state bug as it surfaced?
cases.tonyRaw: I noticed the patches were all shaped the same way: something would go stale or re-render wrong, we'd fix that one call site, and a structurally identical bug would show up somewhere else a week later. That pattern is usually a sign the bug isn't in the code you're editing, it's in the model — we had realtime collaborative data, server-persisted data, and local UI state all living in one undifferentiated store, so any invalidation or update to one could ripple into the others in ways that looked like unrelated one-off bugs. Once I mapped a few of the fixes against each other and saw they all traced back to that same mixing, patching individually stopped making sense. So on Product Forge I solo-owned splitting it into three distinct layers — Liveblocks for realtime, TanStack Query for server-persisted state with proper cache invalidation, and a Context/reducer layer for local UI state — which removed the whole class of bugs instead of chasing instances of it.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Bearer-token auth was a workaround for the cookie-sharing gap between the extension and the main app's domain — did that choice ripple into how you had to handle session expiry or token refresh across 30-plus route handlers, or was it mostly isolated to the auth layer?
cases.tonyRaw: It did ripple beyond the auth layer, yes. Once you're on bearer tokens instead of cookies, the browser isn't handling expiry for you anymore, so every one of those 30-plus route handlers proxying artifact and meeting CRUD needed to agree on what happens when a token goes stale mid-request rather than each one improvising its own behavior. The cleanest way to keep that from becoming 30 slightly different failure modes was to centralize the refresh and expiry handling in one place and have the handlers consume it consistently, so the ripple was real but it didn't mean duplicating auth logic across the surface. It's the kind of decision that looks like "just add a header" until you trace what happens on the unhappy path across every endpoint that depends on it.

cases.interviewerQuestion: You and your co-lead were learning Spanner and Dataflow at the same time as building the migration pipeline on them. What was the hairiest thing that went wrong while you were still finding your footing with those tools, and how did the staged approach catch it?
cases.tonyRaw: The story facts I have don't spell out a specific incident by name, so I don't want to invent one, but I can speak to the shape of it. The riskiest moments came from us still building intuition for Spanner's consistency model and Dataflow's execution semantics while data was actually moving — that combination is exactly where a subtle mismatch between the two systems can silently corrupt or drop records instead of erroring loudly. The staged migration structure is what caught problems before they compounded: we moved data in phases with regression testing at each stage rather than cutting over wholesale, so a discrepancy surfaced against a known-good baseline while it was still small and reversible, instead of after the old system was already gone. That staged discipline was really the whole point of the approach given how new both tools were to us.

cases.interviewerQuestion: What made supporting two concurrent editor versions the hardest part of integrating AI output into ProseMirror's document model, and where did that dual-support requirement force compromises in the state-management design?
cases.tonyRaw: Supporting two editor versions meant every schema decision in the AI output layer had to work against two different sets of node types and marks at once — I couldn't design against ProseMirror's document model as if it were a single fixed target, because the older editor's schema didn't have the same shape as the newer one. That forced the state-management layer I designed to normalize AI output into an intermediate representation before it ever touched either editor's actual document, rather than writing directly against ProseMirror transactions tuned for one schema. The real compromise was velocity: any change to how AI content got inserted had to be validated against both versions, which meant we couldn't take the cleanest single-schema approach and had to carry extra abstraction that only existed to paper over the version gap. I co-led the team of three to four engineers on this, and that state-management design was mine to work through end to end.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Since this was framed as a straight architectural port rather than a shift in where computation happened, what actually made validating calculation accuracy for high-volume trader accounts nontrivial?
cases.tonyRaw: I worked on porting our trade metric computation from a TypeORM-based implementation into our new GraphQL API architecture, validating calculation accuracy with stakeholders along the way. The tricky part wasn't that computation moved somewhere new — it was always server-side — it was that porting the query and aggregation logic into a different data-access layer meant re-deriving the same numbers through a different path, and any subtle difference in how joins, rounding, or filtering happened could silently shift results for accounts with high trade volume. Those accounts are exactly where small discrepancies compound fastest and get noticed first, so I couldn't just eyeball a few sample outputs and call it done. The real work was building enough confidence with stakeholders that the new path produced identical numbers to the old one across enough edge cases and volume levels to trust the cutover.

cases.interviewerQuestion: What made getting that debounce delay right so hard that it took nine months of iteration — were you chasing a moving target of user complaints, or was there some underlying tension between saving too eagerly and saving too late that never fully resolved?
cases.tonyRaw: It was more the underlying tension than chasing complaints — save too eagerly and you're burning cycles and risking writes on every keystroke's worth of dirty state, save too late and a crash or tab close loses real work. There's no fixed number that solves that for every editing pattern, so I kept tuning the delay and the dirty-state tracking in useDebouncedEffect as I saw how people actually used the artifact editor in practice. It wasn't one bug fix, it was closer to nine months of nudging the tradeoff as usage patterns revealed edge cases the previous delay didn't cover.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Before you write code, how do you decide whether a decision needs to be written down first?
cases.tonyRaw: I try to reserve a written decision record for the moments where a choice is hard to reverse, or where the reasoning behind it will matter more than the code itself later — like when there are real tradeoffs between options and picking wrong is expensive to unwind, versus a change that's obviously correct once you see it. I've got a spec on the streamflow forecast pipeline where I laid out the staleness disclosure decision with the options I considered and why I picked the one I did, specifically because the alternative involved a migration and a durability tradeoff that someone six months later would need context on. That habit actually shows up a lot in how I mentor the engineer I work with on Product Forge now — a good chunk of our 1:1s are about helping him recognize which of his own decisions are worth slowing down to document versus which ones he should just make and move on from. If a decision is easily reversible or low-stakes, writing it up is often just overhead.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Have you had a check you wrote keep failing in new ways? What did you change in the end?
cases.tonyRaw: I had exactly this happen on a credential check I was hardening — a pattern matcher that kept catching one bypass only to open a new blind spot, eight rounds running, with each fix dominated by defects the previous round introduced.
